\begin{abstract}
Large-language-model (LLM) trading agents fuse numerical market data with textual signals, which makes them vulnerable to \emph{subtle} misinformation: small edits to sentiment, numbers, causes or entities that remain close to genuine news yet change what the agent does. AutoRedTrader recently showed that such perturbations, generated autonomously and steered by agent feedback, flip a retrieval-based agent's decisions in up to 26.7\% of trading days. We present \rhal{}, an offline, deterministic, CPU-only framework that reproduces the closed-loop red-teaming setting of AutoRedTrader without paid APIs and extends it along four axes: (i)~\emph{stronger temporal evidence}, adding HFT-inspired microstructure proxies (range-based spread, Garman--Klass variance, order-flow imbalance, volume shock, Amihud illiquidity) to the historical-analog grounding signal; (ii)~an \emph{explicit risk-control layer} (confidence gate, hold-on-conflict, volatility-targeted sizing, stop-loss/take-profit, drawdown throttle); (iii)~\emph{strict no-lookahead guarantees} enforced structurally and verified by future-mutation tests, including an admissibility rule for analog outcomes; and (iv)~a \emph{placebo-controlled attack metric}: every attacked run is paired step-by-step with a shadow clean agent, and a placebo arm of meaning-preserving paraphrases measures how many decision flips arise from retrieval-pool perturbation alone. On \val{NseedsRun} paired seeds of synthetic data, the undefended agent shows an attack success rate (ASR) of \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% and a misinformation exposure rate (MER) of \val{MInjectedNoneMER}\% (lift \val{MInjectedNoneMERLift}$\times$ over chance), but the placebo arm alone flips \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\% of decisions, so the misinformation-attributable \emph{net ASR} is \val{CmpNetNone}\% (95\% bootstrap CI \ci{CmpNetNone}). Temporal grounding lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet} against an adaptive attacker and by \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet} against a replay of the attack recorded on the undefended agent, at a cost of \cmp{CmpCostGrounded} in clean return, which we expose as a robustness--return frontier. We detect no further change from adding the microstructure proxies to price-only grounding, from varying the grounding strength, or from adding the risk layer on top of grounding, whether measured by net ASR, by attack-period drawdown or by placebo-corrected \emph{active} flips, a variant we introduce because naive ASR counts the risk layer's defensive Holds as attack successes. Attack-side ablations show that semantic minor perturbations and detector filtering strengthen the attack, whereas style rewriting and strategy feedback raise exposure without a detectable change in net ASR. All code, tests and experiments are reproducible from a single seed. The framework is strictly for defensive robustness evaluation and is not a trading system.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
LLM agents, financial misinformation, red teaming, robustness, time-series grounding, market microstructure, backtesting, risk management
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% =============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
Modern LLM-based financial agents such as FinMem~\cite{yu2025finmem}, FinCon~\cite{yu2024fincon} and TradingAgents~\cite{xiao2025tradingagents} retrieve news from a memory store, reason over it together with market observations, and emit sequential trading actions. Their inputs are therefore an attack surface. Unlike jailbreaks, financial misinformation rarely crosses an explicit safety boundary: a flipped direction word, an inflated percentage, a substituted cause, or a mis-attributed entity produces text that is still \emph{plausible news}, hard to detect without a reference, and yet decision-relevant. AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} formalised this threat as a constrained attack over a finance-theory-structured operator space (behavioural bias, minor semantic perturbation, style rewriting), optimised online with a P\'olya-urn sampler fed by the agent's own decision changes, and reported that time-series-informed grounding partially mitigates it.

Three gaps motivate this project. First, the original evaluation depends on paid LLM calls, real news feeds and FAISS, so a student cannot reproduce it on a laptop. Second, the grounding evidence uses six daily indicators; market microstructure offers additional, faster-moving evidence about whether a textual claim is consistent with what traders are actually doing. Third, the attack success rate (ASR) compares an injected run with a clean run, but \emph{any} change to a retrieval pool reshuffles the top-$k$ documents and can flip near-threshold decisions; without a control, ASR conflates semantic manipulation with retrieval noise.

\textbf{Contributions.} (1)~A compact, fully tested reimplementation of the AutoRedTrader loop that runs offline in mock mode and optionally with any Claude/OpenAI-compatible model. (2)~Microstructure-augmented temporal grounding and an explicit risk layer as defences, ablated individually. (3)~Structural no-lookahead guarantees---trailing normalisation, next-open execution, and an $e+H\le t$ admissibility rule for historical analogs---verified by tests that mutate the future and assert the past is unchanged. (4)~A paired shadow/treated simulation with a placebo arm, yielding \emph{net ASR} and \emph{MER lift}, which we argue are the right quantities to report. (5)~A robustness--return frontier across defence levels, and a 4--5 month roadmap for extending the study.

% =============================================================================
\section{Related Work}
\textbf{LLM trading agents.} FinMem~\cite{yu2025finmem} introduced layered memory and character design; InvestorBench~\cite{li2025investorbench} standardised the Perception/Profile/Memory/Action agent used here; FinCon~\cite{yu2024fincon}, TradingAgents~\cite{xiao2025tradingagents} and FinAgent~\cite{zhang2024finagent} add multi-agent and tool-augmented reasoning. None treat adversarial text as part of the core evaluation.
\textbf{Robustness of financial agents.} TradeTrap~\cite{yan2025tradetrap} shows that small textual changes shift LLM trading decisions substantially. AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} is the first autonomous red-teaming loop specialised to this setting and is our base.
\textbf{Adversarial text and misinformation.} Automated red teaming~\cite{zhou2025autoredteamer}, jailbreak-style prompting~\cite{jiang2024artprompt} and prompt-induced fake-news generation~\cite{wang2026life} target general LLM safety; reference-free counterfactual financial misinformation detection~\cite{jiang2026glisters} shows why subtle edits are hard to flag.
\textbf{Behavioural finance.} Overconfidence~\cite{barber2001boys}, loss aversion~\cite{kahneman2013prospect}, herding~\cite{spyrou2013herding} and noise-trader dynamics~\cite{delong1990noise} ground the bias operator space; the Loughran--McDonald lexicon~\cite{loughran2011liability} motivates our sentiment scorer.
\textbf{Microstructure and backtest validity.} Range-based spread estimators~\cite{corwin2012spread}, Garman--Klass variance~\cite{garman1980estimation}, Amihud illiquidity~\cite{amihud2002illiquidity} and order-flow imbalance~\cite{cont2014price} are the proxies we adopt. Backtest overfitting~\cite{bailey2014probability} and lookahead bias~\cite{lopezdeprado2018advances} inform our no-leak design.

% =============================================================================
\section{Methodology}
\subsection{Problem setting}
Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a corpus of daily news for one asset, $\mathrm{FinAgent}$ a POMDP agent that at each day $t$ retrieves $\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{ret}}_t\subset\mathcal{N}$ and chooses $a_t\in\{\text{Buy},\text{Sell},\text{Hold}\}$. An attacker owns a generator $\mathrm{MisGen}$ that maps clean items to synthetic variants $\tilde{\mathcal{N}}$ and may edit the agent's context $c$ within an accessible region (the system prompt). Following~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}, the attacker seeks a distribution $\pi$ over operators $\phi_{(b,m,r)}$ maximising expected decision change subject to $A_{\mathrm{sim}}(\tilde n,n)\ge\tau_{\mathrm{sim}}$ and $A_{\mathrm{det}}(\tilde n)\le\tau_{\mathrm{det}}$. The defender seeks agent modifications that reduce the induced decision change without discarding useful text.

\subsection{Misinformation generation (MisGen)}
We implement the three operator sub-spaces as deterministic functions of $(n,\text{rng})$ so the loop is reproducible without an LLM (LLM-mode prompts from the paper's Appendix~E are also supported):
\begin{itemize}
\item $\Phi_{\mathrm{Bias}}$: overconfidence, loss aversion, anchoring, herding, confirmation. In LLM mode these are the verbatim prompt templates; in mock mode each maps to an explicit parameter shift of the surrogate policy (Sec.~\ref{sec:agent}) so that $\Phi_{\mathrm{Bias}}$ is measurable.
\item $\Phi_{\mathrm{Minor}}$: flipping (antonym map over directional words and causes), sentiment shift (intensify/dampen), numerical (percentages scaled to $[1.5x,2x]$ or $<0.5x$ preserving direction, as in the paper's rules), temporal (quarter/year shift), entity (company$\to$competitor/subsidiary/parent), concept (revenue$\leftrightarrow$net income, etc.), causal (cause swapped across polarity pools), other (vague attribution).
\item $\Phi_{\mathrm{Rewrite}}$: news style (attribution marker, intensifiers removed, sentences merged) and academic style (formal synonyms, intensifiers$\to$hedges, sentences merged). Both are length-neutral surface transforms that never touch directional words, numbers, entities or causes, i.e.\ they \emph{launder} but cannot undo $\Phi_{\mathrm{Minor}}$.
\item \emph{Placebo} (ours): synonym and connector substitution only; used as the noise-floor control.
\end{itemize}
Strategy selection follows Eqs.~(16)--(18) of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}: $w_s=1+\alpha h_s$, $P(s)=w_s/\sum w$, with a return-dependent boost $\delta$ toward overconfidence when $CR>1$ and loss aversion when $CR<1$. Generation follows Algorithm~1 of the paper with $K$ retries: sample bias with probability $p$; sample $m$; apply Minor; if $(A_{\mathrm{sim}},A_{\mathrm{det}})$ pass, accept; else sample $r$, apply Rewrite, re-check $A_{\mathrm{det}}$.

\textbf{Similarity evaluator.} $A_{\mathrm{sim}}$ is TF-IDF (1--2-gram) cosine similarity with IDF fit once on the clean corpus.
\textbf{Detectability evaluator.} $A_{\mathrm{det}}$ is a logistic regression over 18 interpretable cues (polarity densities, mixed polarity, intensifier/hedge rates, numeric magnitudes, cause--outcome mismatch, sentence structure, entity/ticker presence, vague attribution). It is trained on an \emph{independent} synthetic corpus with positives from $\Phi_{\mathrm{Minor}}$ only, and its threshold is calibrated to a \val{DetFPR}\% false-positive rate on held-out clean text. Training on Minor outputs only mirrors a ``standard detector'' that $\Phi_{\mathrm{Rewrite}}$ is designed to evade; Table~\ref{tab:detector} quantifies the laundering effect.

\subsection{Closed-loop feedback}
After each day the treated agent's action is compared with the shadow clean agent's action on the same day; if they differ, the day's bias and the strategies of every synthetic document that was retrieved are reinforced (Eq.~(7) of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}). Because both agents see the identical market path and differ only in text, this is a genuinely paired update.

\subsection{Temporal grounding with microstructure evidence}
At day $t$ we compute, from rows $\le t$ only: 1-day return, 5-day volatility, 20-day drawdown, short/long trend divergence, a trailing-residual anomaly score and 5/20-day momentum (the paper's Eq.~(19), with residual-$z$ in place of STL because STL is not online-safe); and six microstructure proxies: $(H-L)/C$ spread proxy~\cite{corwin2012spread}, Garman--Klass realised variance~\cite{garman1980estimation}, order-flow imbalance (tick-rule buy/sell volume when intraday bars exist, else close-location value)~\cite{cont2014price}, volume shock, Amihud illiquidity~\cite{amihud2002illiquidity} and range ratio. Features are $z$-scored with a \emph{trailing} 60-day window---full-sample normalisation would leak. A bounded market signal $s_{\mathrm{mkt}}=\tanh(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{z}_t)$ uses fixed, documented weights (no fitting, hence no leakage). Analogs are the top-$k$ cosine neighbours of the flattened 30-day window among windows ending at $e$ with $e+H\le t$, so that each analog's $H$-day forward outcome is already observed at $t$; their mean forward return is blended into $s_{\mathrm{mkt}}$. Consistency between text and market is $c=1-|s_{\mathrm{text}}-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}|/2\in[0,1]$.

\subsection{Agent and defences}\label{sec:agent}
The agent follows InvestorBench/FinMem: \emph{Perception} builds the observation (prices, retrieved documents with provenance labels, evidence); \emph{Profile} holds the task, asset context and the attacker-controlled bias context; \emph{Memory} keeps a working buffer of recent steps with reflections and a long-term text-trust estimate; \emph{Action} maps to Buy/Sell/Hold. Three policies share this interface: a rule baseline (market evidence only), a real LLM (prompt = Perception+Profile+Memory+Evidence+documents, JSON output, disk-cached for reproducibility), and the default \emph{surrogate} policy. The surrogate scores each retrieved document with a negation- and intensity-aware finance lexicon, forms $s_{\mathrm{text}}$ as the retrieval-weighted mean, applies the day's bias as a parameter shift (overconfidence: action threshold $\times0.55$; loss aversion: negative signals $\times1.7$; anchoring: $0.5$ blend with yesterday's signal; herding: pull toward the recent majority action; confirmation: agreeing documents up-weighted), and fuses $s=\lambda s_{\mathrm{text}}+(1-\lambda)s_{\mathrm{mkt}}$ with $\lambda=0.75$ to mirror an LLM's text-heavy reliance. \textbf{Grounding} shrinks inconsistent text toward market evidence,
\begin{equation}
s_g = s-\kappa\,(1-c)\,(s-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}),
\end{equation}
leaving consistent text untouched. \textbf{Risk layer} (post-policy, can only reduce or exit): confidence gate, hold-on-conflict when $c<0.6$, volatility-targeted sizing $\min(1,\sigma^*/\sigma_5)$, 6\%/12\% stop-loss/take-profit, and a 50\% size throttle beyond 10\% drawdown. Every override is logged.

\subsection{Backtester and no-lookahead guarantees}
Decisions at close $t$ execute at open $t+1$ with \val{SlipBps}\,bps slippage and \val{FeeBps}\,bps fees, no leverage, long-only. Accounting invariants ($\mathrm{equity}=\mathrm{cash}+\mathrm{shares}\cdot\mathrm{price}$, cash $\ge0$, round trips lose exactly costs) are unit-tested. Lookahead is excluded structurally (trailing operations, next-open fills, analog admissibility) and verified by tests that multiply all prices after a cut-off by 5, rebuild features, evidence and decisions, and assert bit-identical outputs before the cut-off.

\subsection{Metrics}
MER and ASR follow Eqs.~(8)--(9) of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}. We add: \textbf{MER lift} $=\mathrm{MER}/\bar\rho$ where $\bar\rho$ is the synthetic share of the visible pool (retrieval above chance); \textbf{net ASR} $=\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{inj}}-\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{placebo}}$ computed per seed and defence level; signal deviation $\mathbb{E}|s^{\mathrm{inj}}_t-s^{\mathrm{clean}}_t|$; ASR conditional on exposure; exposure and flips by perturbation type and by bias; cumulative return (CR), maximum drawdown, Sharpe-like ratio, turnover, and risk-override counts.

% =============================================================================
\section{System Architecture}
The package \texttt{rhal} has nine modules with a strict dependency order (data $\to$ features $\to$ grounding; memory; misgen; llm; agent; backtest; evaluation). Every stochastic component draws from a child seed derived by hashing the master seed with a component tag, so changing the number of random draws in MisGen cannot perturb data generation or the shadow agent. A single YAML file holds every knob and ablations are dotted overrides. The simulation loop (\texttt{Simulation.run}) is roughly sixty lines: per day it (1)~lets MisGen sample a bias and inject variants of that day's clean items into the treated pool, (2)~marks both portfolios, (3)~lets the shadow and treated agents perceive, decide and pass through the risk layer, (4)~executes and marks at $t+1$, and (5)~feeds back the paired decision difference. Figures~1--4 of the accompanying repository documentation (\texttt{docs/ARCHITECTURE.md}) give the Mermaid system, class and sequence diagrams. All synthetic text carries \texttt{provenance="synthetic"} and a safety label; no module can route an order.

% =============================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
\textbf{Data.} Because the study must be reproducible offline, we generate a synthetic asset: \val{NDays} business days of OHLCV from a 3-regime Markov drift with GARCH(1,1) volatility~\cite{bollerslev1986garch}, small overnight gaps independent of the day's drift, and \val{NewsPerDay} template news items per day whose latent sentiment is correlated ($\rho=0.35$) with the next-day return, i.e.\ news is genuinely but noisily informative. Templates always contain entities, figures, causes and period references so every $\Phi_{\mathrm{Minor}}$ type has a target. Real OHLCV can be loaded from CSV or \texttt{yfinance}; the last \val{NevalDays} days are evaluated (as in the paper's 60-day BTC window), the rest serve as warm-up and analog library.
\textbf{Arms.} For each of three defence levels---\emph{none} (ungrounded, text-heavy), \emph{grounded} (temporal grounding + microstructure), \emph{grounded+risk}---we run \emph{clean}, \emph{placebo} and \emph{injected} arms, each as a paired shadow/treated simulation, over \val{NseedsRun} seeds. MisGen uses $p=0.7$, $\alpha=1$, $\delta=0.15$, $K=3$, $\tau_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.35$, $\tau_{\mathrm{det}}$ at the calibrated threshold, injection ratio 1:1; retrieval is TF-IDF top-\val{TopK} over the last 3 days with recency decay; $\kappa=\val{Kappa}$.
\textbf{Attack settings.} Defences are evaluated against two attackers. In the \emph{adaptive} setting MisGen runs live and its feedback loop adapts to the defended agent. In the \emph{frozen} setting the attack recorded against the undefended agent of the same seed (documents and daily bias contexts) is replayed verbatim against every defence, so differences between frozen arms are caused by the defence alone. MisGen draws its randomness from streams keyed by (seed, day, item), so all arms of a seed share the attacker's random numbers (common random numbers) and no result depends on an arm's label.
\textbf{Statistics.} All arms of a seed share the market path and clean news, so every comparison is paired by seed. For each claim we report the mean per-seed difference with a 95\% percentile-bootstrap confidence interval over seeds and a two-sided sign-flip permutation $p$-value, Holm-corrected within each family of related comparisons (Tables~\ref{tab:stats_main} and~\ref{tab:stats_ablation}). In the text, ``$\Delta$\,pp~[lo,~hi]'' is the mean paired difference in percentage points with its 95\% CI. The CIs are not adjusted for multiplicity, so we call a difference detectable only if its CI excludes zero \emph{and} $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.05$; otherwise we report no detectable difference.
\textbf{Ablations.} Attack-side (w/o filtering, feedback, bias, minor, rewrite) against the undefended agent, mirroring the paper's Table~2; defence-side (none, grounding only, grounding+micro, risk only, full, w/o hold-on-conflict); retrieval breadth $k\in\{2,4,8\}$; grounding strength $\kappa\in\{0.3,0.7,1.0\}$.
\textbf{Compute.} Everything runs single-process on a laptop CPU at about half a second per paired 60-day run; the main experiment (12 arms $\times$ \val{NseedsRun} seeds) takes a few minutes.

\section{Results}
\IfFileExists{tables/main_results.tex}{\input{tables/main_results.tex}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/stats_main.tex}{\input{tables/stats_main.tex}}{}
\textbf{Attack effectiveness} (Table~\ref{tab:main}). Against the undefended agent the injected arm reaches MER \val{MInjectedNoneMER}\% (lift \val{MInjectedNoneMERLift}$\times$: rewritten documents acquire ticker mentions and finance markers that make them \emph{more} retrievable than chance) and ASR \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\,$\pm$\,\val{MInjectedNoneASRSd}\%. This naive rate is higher than the 26.7\% reported on BTC by~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}, but the two are not directly comparable: our asset and news are synthetic, our agent is a surrogate policy, our operators are rule-based, and neither rate is corrected for the placebo effect described next. Signal deviation is \val{MInjectedNoneSignalDeviation}\,$\pm$\,\val{MInjectedNoneSignalDeviationSd} versus \val{MPlaceboNoneSignalDeviation}\,$\pm$\,\val{MPlaceboNoneSignalDeviationSd} for placebo, so misinformation moves the agent's internal signal further than paraphrase does.

\textbf{The placebo control.} The placebo arm---paraphrases that preserve every number, entity and direction---nevertheless flips \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\% of decisions. Inspection shows that on almost every evaluation day the top-$k$ set differs between shadow and treated agents once the pool doubles: near-duplicates displace other documents, the text signal is averaged over fewer sources, and a sizeable share of clean-arm signals lie within 0.05 of the action threshold. The misinformation-attributable \emph{net} ASR is therefore \val{CmpNetNone}\% \ci{CmpNetNone}, and the net rate of \emph{active} flips (treated agent trades, clean agent did something else) is \val{CmpActnetNone}\% \ci{CmpActnetNone}. We regard this as a central methodological finding: naive ASR overstates the semantic effect of subtle misinformation by roughly a factor of two on our data, and a paraphrase control should accompany any reported ASR.

\textbf{Defences.} Grounding lowers naive ASR from \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% to \val{MInjectedGroundedASR}\% (\cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedAsr}) and net ASR by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet} (\pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet}). Part of the naive gain is lower sensitivity to \emph{any} perturbation of the pool---grounding also lowers placebo ASR, by \cmp{CmpPlaceboGrounded}---but the net gain, and a reduction of \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedActnet} in placebo-corrected active flips (\pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedActnet}), show that it also removes misinformation-specific flips. The gain does not depend on the attacker adapting to the defence: against the frozen attack, grounding lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet} (\pholm{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet}) and net active flips by \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedActnet} (\pholm{CmpGainFrozenGroundedActnet}). Grounding does not neutralise the attack, however: the grounded agent's net ASR is still \val{CmpNetGrounded}\% \ci{CmpNetGrounded}. Adding the risk layer on top of grounding produces no detectable difference in net ASR (reduction \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskNet}, \pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskNet}), in placebo-corrected active flips (reduction \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskActnet}, \pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskActnet}) or in attack-period maximum drawdown (\val{MInjectedGroundedRiskMaxDrawdown}\% vs \val{MInjectedGroundedMaxDrawdown}\%; difference \cmp{CmpDdRisk}, \pholm{CmpDdRisk}), and the frozen attack gives the same result for net ASR and net active flips (Table~\ref{tab:stats_main}). With the risk layer added, even the reduction in net active flips relative to the undefended agent is no longer detectable (\cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedRiskActnet}, \pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedRiskActnet}). Naive ASR is higher with the risk layer than with grounding alone (\val{MInjectedGroundedRiskASR}\% vs \val{MInjectedGroundedASR}\%) because \texttt{hold\_on\_conflict} fires on the treated agent whenever injected text conflicts with market evidence, and Eq.~(9) counts that defensive Hold as a decision change; the active-flip variant removes this artefact but still shows no benefit. The cost of grounding is visible in the paired clean return: \val{MCleanNoneCR}\% undefended versus \val{MCleanGroundedCR}\% grounded and \val{MCleanGroundedRiskCR}\% with risk controls, a loss of \cmp{CmpCostGrounded} and \cmp{CmpCostGroundedRisk} respectively, because the synthetic news is genuinely informative and grounding discounts it whenever it disagrees with lagging market evidence. Figure~\ref{fig:frontier} plots this robustness--return frontier; Fig.~\ref{fig:equity} shows seed-0 equity curves and Fig.~\ref{fig:exposure} the exposure and flips by perturbation type.

\section{Ablation Study}
\IfFileExists{tables/ablation_attack.tex}{\input{tables/ablation_attack.tex}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/ablation_defense.tex}{\input{tables/ablation_defense.tex}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/ablation_retrieval.tex}{\input{tables/ablation_retrieval.tex}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/ablation_grounding_strength.tex}{\input{tables/ablation_grounding_strength.tex}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/detector.tex}{\input{tables/detector.tex}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/stats_ablation.tex}{\input{tables/stats_ablation.tex}}{}
\textbf{Attack components} (Table~\ref{tab:abl_attack}). Against the undefended agent, two components detectably strengthen the attack. Removing \emph{minor} perturbation lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpAblAttackWoMinorNet} (\pholm{CmpAblAttackWoMinorNet}; \val{AblAttackInjectedWoMinorASRNet}\% vs \val{AblAttackInjectedFullASRNet}\% full), so semantic edits are a major source of the attack. Removing \emph{filtering} lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpAblAttackWoFilteringNet} (\pholm{CmpAblAttackWoFilteringNet}) and MER by \cmp{CmpAblAttackWoFilteringMer}. Without filtering the first Minor candidate is always accepted, so nothing is screened or rewritten, and the causal and vague-attribution edits that the detector almost always flags (Table~\ref{tab:detector}) are no longer rejected in favour of less detectable flipping, sentiment and numerical edits. Removing the \emph{bias} context or the \emph{feedback} loop produces no detectable difference in net ASR (\cmp{CmpAblAttackWoBiasNet}, \pholm{CmpAblAttackWoBiasNet}; \cmp{CmpAblAttackWoFeedbackNet}, \pholm{CmpAblAttackWoFeedbackNet}). Feedback does raise MER, by \cmp{CmpAblAttackWoFeedbackMer}: the P\'olya-urn update reinforces only strategies whose documents were retrieved, so it learns what gets retrieved, but with a placebo floor of \val{AblAttackPlaceboFullASR}\% its flip signal is plausibly too noisy to learn what changes decisions. Likewise, \emph{rewriting} raises MER by \cmp{CmpAblAttackWoRewriteMer} but produces no detectable difference in net ASR (\cmp{CmpAblAttackWoRewriteNet}, \pholm{CmpAblAttackWoRewriteNet}): with rule-based operators, laundering makes documents more retrievable and, for most edit types, less detectable (Table~\ref{tab:detector}) without a detectable gain in decision impact. Whether the LLM rewrites of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} behave differently can be tested with the same harness in LLM mode. Every row is accompanied by its own placebo (bottom half of the table), which is flat across variants as it should be.

\textbf{Defence components} (Table~\ref{tab:abl_defense}). The robustness gain comes from grounding itself: price-only grounding lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveGrounding} against the adaptive attacker (\pholm{CmpAblDefAdaptiveGrounding}) and by \cmp{CmpAblDefFrozenGrounding} against the frozen one (\pholm{CmpAblDefFrozenGrounding}). Adding the microstructure proxies has no detectable effect in either setting (reductions of \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveMicro}, \pholm{CmpAblDefAdaptiveMicro}, and \cmp{CmpAblDefFrozenMicro}, \pholm{CmpAblDefFrozenMicro}). In our generator, high, low and volume are functions of the simulated return and volatility plus independent noise, so the proxies add no directional information beyond the price series; whether real order-flow data behave differently is untested. The risk layer alone lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveRiskAlone} against the adaptive attacker (\pholm{CmpAblDefAdaptiveRiskAlone}), even though its defensive Holds raise naive ASR (\val{AblDefenseInjectedRiskOnlyASR}\% vs \val{AblDefenseInjectedNoneASR}\%); against the frozen attack the reduction is not detectable (\cmp{CmpAblDefFrozenRiskAlone}, \pholm{CmpAblDefFrozenRiskAlone}). On top of grounding, neither the risk layer nor its hold-on-conflict rule has a detectable effect on net ASR (reductions of \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveRiskOnTop} and \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveHold} against the adaptive attacker, \cmp{CmpAblDefFrozenRiskOnTop} and \cmp{CmpAblDefFrozenHold} against the frozen one; none significant after Holm correction).

\textbf{Retrieval breadth} (Table~\ref{tab:abl_retrieval}). Net ASR shows no detectable dependence on $k$ (\val{AblRetrievalInjectedKTwoASRNet}\%, \val{AblRetrievalInjectedKFourASRNet}\% and \val{AblRetrievalInjectedKEightASRNet}\% for $k=2,4,8$; $k=2$ minus $k=4$: \cmp{CmpAblRetKTwoNet}, \pholm{CmpAblRetKTwoNet}; $k=8$ minus $k=4$: \cmp{CmpAblRetKEightNet}, \pholm{CmpAblRetKEightNet}), so we find no evidence that the net metric is an artefact of a particular $k$. The noise floor itself does depend on $k$: placebo ASR is lower at $k=8$ than at $k=4$ (difference \cmp{CmpAblRetKEightPlacebo}, \pholm{CmpAblRetKEightPlacebo}), consistent with the placebo mechanism described in the Results, since averaging the text signal over more documents makes it less sensitive to which near-duplicates enter the top-$k$; $k=2$ and $k=4$ do not differ detectably (\cmp{CmpAblRetKTwoPlacebo}, \pholm{CmpAblRetKTwoPlacebo}).

\textbf{Grounding strength} (Table~\ref{tab:abl_grounding_strength}). Within the full defence, neither step of the $\kappa$ sweep has a detectable effect. The reductions in net ASR from raising $\kappa$ from 0.3 to 0.7 and from 0.7 to 1.0 are \cmp{CmpAblKappaAdaptiveZeropThreeZeropSeven} and \cmp{CmpAblKappaAdaptiveZeropSevenOnepZero} against the adaptive attacker and \cmp{CmpAblKappaFrozenZeropThreeZeropSeven} and \cmp{CmpAblKappaFrozenZeropSevenOnepZero} against the frozen one; the corresponding clean-return costs are \cmp{CmpAblKappaCostZeropThreeZeropSeven} and \cmp{CmpAblKappaCostZeropSevenOnepZero}; none is significant after Holm correction. Each step is far smaller than the effect of switching grounding on (\cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet} in net ASR for \cmp{CmpCostGrounded} of clean return), so over the range tested the frontier of Fig.~\ref{fig:frontier} is set by whether grounding is used, not by how strongly it shrinks inconsistent text.

\textbf{Detector} (Table~\ref{tab:detector}). The proxy reaches \val{DetAcc} training accuracy at a \val{DetFPR}\% clean false-positive rate; temporal and numerical edits are nearly undetectable (\val{DetTemporalMinor}\% and \val{DetNumericalMinor}\%), entity/concept/causal edits are the most detectable, and both rewrite styles reduce detection for every type except the ``other'' category, reproducing the paper's ``Minor produces, Rewrite launders'' dynamic.

% =============================================================================
\section{Safety and Ethics}
This work generates synthetic financial misinformation for the sole purpose of measuring and improving agent robustness. Every generated record carries a mandatory provenance label and a safety string; text never leaves the simulator except into labelled, git-ignored logs; there is no broker, order-routing or live-data path; the attacker's objective is decision change, not profit, and no code steers prices or disseminates content. The framework should not be used on real news feeds, for investment advice, or in any live setting, and our synthetic entities are fictitious. We follow the dual-use discussion of~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} and release the code to support defensive research.

% =============================================================================
\section{Limitations}
(1)~The default agent is a transparent surrogate rather than an LLM; the harness supports LLM mode but our headline numbers are surrogate-based. (2)~Data and news are synthetic; template news is more regular than real reporting, which likely makes the lexical detector both easier to train and easier to fool. (3)~The detectability proxy is a small feature classifier, not an LLM judge. (4)~Stop-loss/take-profit are evaluated at daily closes. (5)~Sixty evaluation days per seed makes CR noisy; we therefore base claims on paired per-seed differences with bootstrap confidence intervals and permutation tests over \val{NseedsRun} seeds rather than on single-run returns. (6)~Placebo ASR reveals that a threshold policy over retrieved-document averages is intrinsically jittery; smoother policies (hysteresis, probabilistic actions) would change both naive and net ASR.

% =============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\rhal{} turns the AutoRedTrader red-teaming loop into a reproducible, offline laboratory and extends it with microstructure-augmented grounding, an explicit risk layer, structural no-lookahead guarantees and a placebo-controlled attack metric. Over \val{NseedsRun} paired seeds the undefended agent is measurably vulnerable (net ASR \val{CmpNetNone}\% \ci{CmpNetNone}), but the placebo arm alone flips \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\% of decisions against a naive ASR of \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\%, so more than half of naive attack success reflects retrieval-pool perturbation rather than the meaning of the injected text. Temporal grounding buys robustness at a quantified cost: it lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet} against an adaptive attacker and by \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet} against a frozen one, for \cmp{CmpCostGrounded} of clean return. Beyond that we detect no gain from the microstructure proxies over price-only grounding, from the grounding strength $\kappa$, or from the risk layer, whose defensive Holds naive ASR mis-scores as attack successes. With rule-based operators, semantic minor perturbations and detector filtering drive the attack, while style rewriting raises exposure without a detectable change in net ASR; whether LLM rewrites behave differently is a question the harness makes easy to test with a real model. Future work will run the same harness with real LLM policies and real price series, add smoother action policies, and study directional (profit-seeking) attackers under the same safety boundary.
